abstract: Oxidative stress is a common challenge in intensive duck production systems, often disrupting intestinal barrier integrity and compromising animal health. This study aimed to explore how oxidative stress alters the secretion and protein cargo of extracellular vesicles ( EVs ) derived from duck intestinal epithelial cells ( IECs ), which are crucial mediators of epithelial communication and stress adaptation. Duck IECs were exposed to increasing concentrations of hydrogen peroxide (0–200 μmol/L) to induce oxidative stress. EVs were then isolated and characterized using electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking, and protein cargo was analyzed via 4D label-free proteomics. The results revealed that oxidative stress caused dose-dependent cytotoxicity and suppressed gene expression patterns linked to barrier function and the oxidative stress response ( P < 0.05). Interestingly, low-to-moderate oxidative stress (50–100 μmol/L) increased EV secretion, whereas higher doses (200 μmol/L) reduced it ( P < 0.05). Proteomic analysis revealed that the differentially expressed proteins in EVs were associated with RNA metabolism, redox balance, protein folding, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Notably, EVs from moderately stressed cells were enriched in chaperones (e.g., HSP90AB1 and CALR) and lipid-binding proteins (e.g., FABP5), which may influence epithelial–stem cell signaling. Transcription factor analysis revealed that XBP1, SP1, and BHLHE40 are key regulators of these proteomic changes. In conclusion, oxidative stress modulates both the release and molecular cargo characteristics of EVs in duck IECs in a dose-dependent manner, potentially impairing their signaling roles in intestinal homeostasis. These findings provide mechanistic insights into EV-mediated epithelial communication under stress and suggest potential targets for antioxidant interventions in poultry production systems.

Materials and methods
Animal ethics statement
All procedures involving animals were carried out in compliance with the Laboratory Animal Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Science and Technology. The experimental protocol was reviewed and approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Hubei Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Approval No. 2021-620-000-001-021).
Cultivation and oxidative stress induction in IECs
The isolation and culture of duck IECs were performed with reference to the method previously described by
Zhang et al. (2019)
, with minor modifications. In brief, small intestinal tissues were collected from 26-day-old duck embryos during the pipping stage under sterile conditions. Approximately 5 cm of the intestine was excised, and mesenteric tissue and pancreas were carefully removed. The tissue segments were rinsed thoroughly in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, Biosharp, Hefei, Anhui, China) containing penicillin (100 U/mL) and streptomycin (100 μg/mL) (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) to minimize contamination. Following mechanical dissociation, the tissue was finely minced and enzymatically digested in 1 % type I collagenase (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) at 37 °C for 70 minutes with gentle agitation every 10 minutes. Upon completion of digestion, the reaction was terminated by removing the supernatant, and the tissue fragments were gently triturated in PBS to obtain a single-cell suspension. Cells were then collected by centrifugation at 1000 rpm for 3 minutes and resuspended in modified DMEM/F12 (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) medium containing 5 % fetal bovine serum (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and 100 ng/mL epidermal growth factor (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The suspension was filtered through a 100 μm cell strainer (Biosharp, Hefei, Anhui, China) and seeded in 6-well plates (Corning, Corning Inc., Corning, NY, USA) at a density of 3 × 10⁵ cells/cm². The cells were maintained at 37 °C with 5 % CO₂ in a humidified incubator for 24 hours.
After reaching confluence, cells were randomly divided into four groups based on hydrogen peroxide (
H₂O₂
) treatment concentrations: a control group (0 μmol/L H₂O₂), a low-concentration group (50 μmol/L H₂O₂), a medium-concentration group (100 μmol/L H₂O₂), and a high-concentration group (200 μmol/L H₂O₂). Each group was treated with the respective H₂O₂ concentration for 6 hours to induce oxidative stress in duck IECs. Post-treatment, cell morphology was observed under an inverted microscope (Nikon Eclipse Ts2, Nikon Instruments Inc., Tokyo, Japan). In parallel, cells were harvested for RNA extraction and gene expression analysis, and the corresponding culture supernatants were collected for EV isolation. The H₂O₂ concentration gradient was selected based on previous studies (Zhang, et al., 2019).
Cell viability
Cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo Molecular Technologies, Kumamoto, Japan). Briefly, cells were seeded into 96-well plates (Corning, Corning Inc., Corning, NY, USA) at a density of 2 × 10³ cells per well and subjected to treatment with 0, 50, 100, or 200 μmol/L H₂O₂ for 6 hours. Following treatment, 20 μL of CCK-8 solution was added to each well, and the plates were incubated at 37 °C for 4 hours. Absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (Synergy H1, BioTek Instruments, Winooski, VT, USA). Each treatment group was tested in six technical replicates.
Cell viability was calculated using the following formula:
[(OD_treatment − OD_blank) / (OD_control − OD_blank)] × 100 %
Total RNA extraction and reverse transcription
Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (ABclonal Biotechnology Co., Ltd., Wuhan, China). Briefly, cells were lysed in TRIzol and centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4 °C to remove cellular debris. The supernatant was transferred to a new tube and mixed vigorously with 200 μL chloroform until a milky emulsion formed. After phase separation by centrifugation (12,000 rpm, 15 minutes, 4 °C), the aqueous phase was collected and mixed gently with 500 μL isopropanol. The mixture was incubated on ice for 20 minutes, followed by RNA precipitation via centrifugation at 12,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4 °C. The RNA pellet was washed once with 75 % ethanol (prepared with DEPC-treated water) and once with pre-chilled 100 % ethanol, air-dried at room temperature for 5–7 minutes, and dissolved in 30–100 μL of DEPC-treated water. RNA concentration and integrity were assessed using a NanoPhotometer spectrophotometer (Implen GmbH, Munich, Germany) and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer system (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA), respectively. RNA was frozen at −80 °C post-purification for later use. Complementary DNA was synthesized from 1 μg total RNA using the HiScript III RT SuperMix kit (+gDNA wiper; Vazyme, Nanjing, China) in a 20 μL system. Synthesized cDNA was preserved at −20 °C for subsequent use.
qRT-PCR analysis of intestinal barrier and oxidative stress–related genes
To evaluate gene expression related to intestinal barrier integrity and oxidative stress response, the mRNA levels of tight junction–associated genes, including zonula occludens-1 (
ZO-1
), Claudin-1, and Occludin, as well as oxidative stress–responsive genes, namely nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (
Nrf2
) and heme oxygenase-1 (
HO-1
), were quantified. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (
GAPDH
) was used as the internal reference gene. Primer sequences were designed using the NCBI Primer-BLAST tool and synthesized by Sangon Biotech Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) (
Table 1
). qRT-PCR amplification was carried out employing the SYBR Premix Ex Taq kit (Vazyme Biotech Co., Ltd., Nanjing, China) on a LightCycler real-time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Expression differences were evaluated using the 2^
−ΔΔCt
quantitative method.

Extracellular vesicle isolation
EVs were isolated from cell culture supernatants using a standard differential ultracentrifugation protocol. Briefly, serum-free conditioned media were collected from each treatment group after 6 h of oxidative stress induction. The supernatant was subjected to sequential centrifugation steps at 300 × g for 10 min, 2,000 × g for 10 min, and 10,000 × g for 30 min at 4 °C to remove cells and cellular debris. The resulting supernatant was processed through a 0.22 μm pore membrane filter (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA) to eliminate larger vesicles and apoptotic bodies. The filtered supernatant was carefully layered onto a 30 % sucrose cushion and ultracentrifuged at 100,000 × g for 90 min at 4 °C using a Beckman Optima XPN-100 ultracentrifuge equipped with a Type 70 Ti rotor (Beckman Coulter, Brea, CA, USA). EVs were collected from the sucrose interface, resuspended in PBS, and purified via a second high-speed spin at 100,000 × g for 90 min at 4 °C. EV pellets were reconstituted in 100 μL of PBS and preserved at −80 °C for subsequent analyses. For particle counting, an equal volume of conditioned medium was processed for each condition and EV concentration was reported without cell-number normalization. This approach was selected to capture the overall EV release per condition, encompassing concurrent effects on cell survival and secretion activity.
Transmission electron microscopy
The morphology of isolated EVs was examined by transmission electron microscopy (
TEM
). Briefly, EV samples were fixed with 2 % paraformaldehyde and 2.5 % glutaraldehyde in 0.1 M phosphate buffer (pH 7.4) at 4 °C for 2 h. Samples were rinsed post-fixation, dehydrated with increasing ethanol concentrations, and subsequently embedded in Epon 812 epoxy resin (SPI Supplies, West Chester, PA, USA). Ultrathin sections (70–90 nm) were prepared using an ultramicrotome and mounted onto copper grids. Sections were stained with 2 % uranyl acetate and lead citrate (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) and imaged using a Hitachi HT7800 transmission electron microscope (Hitachi High-Technologies, Tokyo, Japan) operated at 80 kV.
Nanoparticle tracking analysis
The size distribution and particle concentration of EVs were analyzed using nanoparticle tracking analysis (
NTA
) with a NanoSight NS300 system (Malvern Panalytical, Malvern, UK). EV samples were diluted in sterile PBS to a final concentration of approximately 1 × 10⁸ particles/mL before analysis. The suspension was injected into the sample chamber, and particles were visualized using a 532 nm laser. For each sample, three 60-second videos were recorded under constant flow conditions. Data were processed using NTA software to determine particle size and concentration profiles.
Proteomic sample preparation and 4D-DIA analysis
EV samples were homogenized in lysis buffer enriched with 1 mM PMSF and protease inhibitors (Beyotime Biotechnology, Shanghai, China), then subjected to ultrasonic disruption on ice. After centrifugation (15,000 ×
g
, 10 min, 4 °C), supernatants were harvested. Protein levels were measured with a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). After quantification, samples were lyophilized and stored at –80 °C. Proteomic sample preparation and 4D label-free DIA-based proteomic sequencing were outsourced to Wuhan Metware Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). A NanoElute UHPLC platform (Bruker, Bremen) equipped with a C18 column (IonOpticks, 25 cm × 75 μm, 1.6 μm particle size) was employed to separate peptides. The flow rate was set to 300 nL/min at a column temperature of 50 °C. The mobile phase was composed of 0.1 % formic acid in water (A) and in acetonitrile (B), with the gradient as follows: 2–22 % B (0–45 min), 22–35 % B (45–50 min), 35–80 % B (50–55 min), and 80 % B hold (55–60 min). Data acquisition was performed on a timsTOF Pro2 mass spectrometer (Bruker) operated in positive ion mode. Spectral library generation was performed with ddaPASEF scanning, followed by diaPASEF acquisition for quantification. The scan range was set to m/z 400–1200 with an ion mobility window of 1/K₀ = 0.7–1.4 V·s/cm², a cycle time of 1.8 s, and a collision energy of 42 eV.
Bioinformatic analysis
Raw mass spectrometry data were analyzed using DIA-NN software in library-free mode or the annotation of peptide and protein sequences. Label-free quantification was conducted based on the MaxLFQ algorithm to normalize protein abundance across all samples. DEPs were identified using one-way ANOVA with a fold change threshold of ≥1.2 and
P
< 0.05. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and proteins with a false discovery rate (FDR) under 0.05 were deemed statistically significant. Functional annotation and enrichment analyses were conducted using the Gene Ontology (
GO
) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (
KEGG
) databases. Enriched biological processes, cellular components, molecular functions, and signaling pathways were identified through hypergeometric testing considering P-values below 0.05 as statistically significant. To ensure consistency across analyses, all identified proteins were annotated via the UniProt Knowledgebase and converted to standardized gene symbols for subsequent analyses.
Protein-protein interaction analysis
The STRING database (
https://cn.string-db.org
) was employed to build the protein–protein interaction (
PPI
) network, with interaction confidence set to medium (score > 0.4). Interaction data were visualized and analyzed using Cytoscape (version 3.10.3).
Transcription factor prediction analysis of DEPs
To further investigate upstream regulatory mechanisms, transcription factor (
TF
) enrichment analysis was performed using gene sets corresponding to each expression cluster of DEPs. TF prediction was conducted through ChEA3 (
https://maayanlab.cloud/chea3
). For each cluster, the top 10 significantly enriched TFs were selected based on combined ranking scores. TF–target interaction networks were constructed using Cytoscape software (version 3.10.3) to visualize regulatory modules potentially involved in oxidative stress induced proteomic alterations.
Statistical analysis
All experimental data were analyzed using SPSS statistics 26.0 software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Data normality was examined with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and homogeneity of variances was assessed with the Levene test. When assumptions were met, one-way ANOVA was used to compare differences among the four treatment groups, followed by Tukey’s HSD post hoc test to identify pairwise differences. When assumptions were not satisfied, the Kruskal–Wallis test was applied. Statistical significance was defined as
P
< 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Graph generation was performed with GraphPad Prism 9.5.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).
body:
Introduction
In modern duck farming, cage-rearing systems are being rapidly adopted for both meat and egg production. However, ducks are naturally timid and highly sensitive to disturbances. Under intensive management conditions, routine practices such as vaccination, daily inspection, and exposure to environmental stressors such as high temperature and humidity frequently trigger stress responses in flocks (
Zhang et al., 2019b
;
Zheng, et al., 2022
). As ducks are increasingly placed in caged environments, often referred to as "forcing ducks onto racks", their adaptability to such settings has become a central research issue related to duck breeding and environmental physiology (
Bai, et al., 2022
;
He, et al., 2024
). Stress can lead to endogenous damage across various organs, with the intestines, being particularly vulnerable as primary target organ (
Tian, et al., 2025
). Under stress, intestinal blood flow can decrease by as much as 40 to 50 %, subjecting villus epithelial cells to both physiological and pathological hypoxia. This results in an excessive accumulation of reactive oxygen species (
ROS
), initiating varying degrees of oxidative stress and mucosal injury (
Mishra and Jha, 2019
;
Yang, et al., 2021
), which in turn severely impairs both the health and productivity of the flock. Mild damage may be repaired through the intrinsic healing mechanisms of the gut, which involve a range of cellular processes such as epithelial regeneration and migration (
Montenegro-Miranda, et al., 2020
), immune‒epithelial cooperation (
Guenin-Macé, et al., 2022
), extracellular matrix remodeling (
Sprangers, et al., 2021
), and the regulation of oxidative and antioxidative pathways (
Zhang, et al., 2023
). However, intense oxidative stress can disrupt the tight junctions between intestinal epithelial cells (
IECs
), induce apoptosis, and compromise intestinal barrier function. This leads to impaired nutrient absorption and immune dysfunction (
Ivison, et al., 2010
;
Paradis, et al., 2021
), ultimately reducing feed conversion efficiency and growth performance in laying ducks (
Muro, et al., 2024
) and posing serious threats to their overall health.
Extracellular vesicles (
EVs
) are lipid bilayer-enclosed particles secreted by cells that carry a diverse array of bioactive molecules, including proteins, nucleic acids, and lipids. They play pivotal roles in intercellular communication and the regulation of various physiological processes (
Rani, et al., 2023
). EVs have recently emerged as important players in gut health research, particularly because of their roles in modulating the gut microbiota, alleviating inflammation, and promoting mucosal repair (
Kim, et al., 2024
;
Wang, et al., 2024
;
Yang, et al., 2022
). Emerging studies have suggested that EVs contribute to the maintenance of intestinal barrier function and immune homeostasis through the delivery of regulatory molecules such as microRNAs and heat shock proteins. These molecules can suppress the expression of immune-activating cytokines and enhance intestinal defense mechanisms (
Appiah, et al., 2020
;
Gu, et al., 2021
;
Jiang, et al., 2016
). Despite these advances, the specific roles of EVs derived from duck IECs in the context of endogenous injury repair remain poorly understood, and systematic investigations in this area are still lacking.
IECs are the most abundant cell type within the intestinal mucosa and play a central role in the stress response, particularly under oxidative stress conditions. These cells exhibit heightened sensitivity to oxidative insults and serve as a primary source of EV secretion in the gut environment (
Leoni, et al., 2015
;
Ma, et al., 2017
). Oxidative stress significantly alters the dynamics of EV biogenesis and release. Such stress activates the NF-κB and HIF-1α signaling pathways, both of which are involved in hypoxic responses, ultimately promoting the secretion of EVs (
Chu, et al., 2023
;
Steiner, et al., 2022
;
Zheng, et al., 2015
). Conversely, the activation of autophagic pathways may suppress EV release through the degradation of multivesicular bodies, the key intermediates in EV formation (
Zhu, et al., 2020
). Previous investigations revealed that IEC-derived EVs play crucial roles in intercellular communication during mucosal injury repair (
Shami-Shah, et al., 2023
;
Xu, et al., 2023
). However, the specific characteristics of EV secretion by duck IECs under oxidative stress, such as their release patterns, functional molecular cargo, and underlying mechanisms mediating mucosal regeneration remain insufficiently explored. Further in-depth investigations are therefore warranted.
Owing to an inherently limited EV yield, conventional proteomic techniques often lead to challenges in terms of sensitivity and detection (
Shami-Shah, Norman and Walt, 2023
). Recently, the emergence of 4D proteomics has offered a powerful next-generation approach for protein profiling. Building upon traditional 3D proteomic technologies, which rely on retention time, mass-charge ratio (m/z), and ion intensity 4D proteomics introduces ion mobility as a fourth analytical dimension. This additional parameter enables the separation of precursor ions on the basis of their collision cross-section, significantly increasing resolution and peptide identification. By employing multidimensional separation strategies, 4D proteomics markedly improves ion transmission efficiency and detection sensitivity. When combined with deep-coverage mass spectrometry acquisition modes, it allows for precise quantitative analysis of protein samples at the nanogram level, rendering it a transformative tool for profiling dynamic changes in EV proteomes (
Deng, et al., 2023
;
Luo, et al., 2025
;
Xie, et al., 2024
). Recent studies have demonstrated that 4D proteomics can overcome the traditional limitations associated with profiling low-abundance proteins. For example, compared with previous methods, this approach has enabled the detection of tight junction (
TJ
) and anti-inflammatory repair-associated proteins such as claudin-3 and annexin A1 in EV samples, resulting in significantly higher protein identification rates (
Sun, et al., 2021
). These advances suggest that the high-resolution separation and ultrasensitive detection capabilities of 4D proteomics make it an ideal platform for elucidating the functional protein landscapes of EVs and complex molecular interaction networks.
In this study, we employed duck IECs as a model to systematically investigate how oxidative stress affects EV secretion and proteomic composition in an in vitro induction system. Using ultrasensitive, microscale 4D proteomic analysis, we identified differentially expressed proteins (
DEPs
) and applied bioinformatic approaches to analyze the signaling pathways involved. This work aims to elucidate the mechanisms by which oxidative stress modulates EV-mediated mucosal injury and repair, thus providing conceptual support for the design of antioxidative approaches targeting EVs to increase poultry gut health and production efficiency.

Proteomic sample preparation and 4D label-free DIA-based proteomic sequencing were outsourced to Wuhan Metware Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Wuhan, China). The flow rate was set to 300 nL/min at a column temperature of 50 °C. The mobile phase was composed of 0.1 % formic acid in water (A) and in acetonitrile (B), with the gradient as follows: 2–22 % B (0–45 min), 22–35 % B (45–50 min), 35–80 % B (50–55 min), and 80 % B hold (55–60 min). Data acquisition was performed on a timsTOF Pro2 mass spectrometer (Bruker) operated in positive ion mode. Spectral library generation was performed with ddaPASEF scanning, followed by diaPASEF acquisition for quantification. The scan range was set to m/z 400–1200 with an ion mobility window of 1/K₀ = 0.7–1.4 V·s/cm², a cycle time of 1.8 s, and a collision energy of 42 eV.
Bioinformatic analysis
Raw mass spectrometry data were analyzed using DIA-NN software in library-free mode or the annotation of peptide and protein sequences. Label-free quantification was conducted based on the MaxLFQ algorithm to normalize protein abundance across all samples. DEPs were identified using one-way ANOVA with a fold change threshold of ≥1.2 and
P
< 0.05. Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure, and proteins with a false discovery rate (FDR) under 0.05 were deemed statistically significant. Functional annotation and enrichment analyses were conducted using the Gene Ontology (
GO
) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (
KEGG
) databases. Enriched biological processes, cellular components, molecular functions, and signaling pathways were identified through hypergeometric testing considering P-values below 0.05 as statistically significant. To ensure consistency across analyses, all identified proteins were annotated via the UniProt Knowledgebase and converted to standardized gene symbols for subsequent analyses.
Protein-protein interaction analysis
The STRING database (
https://cn.string-db.org
) was employed to build the protein–protein interaction (
PPI
) network, with interaction confidence set to medium (score > 0.4). Interaction data were visualized and analyzed using Cytoscape (version 3.10.3).
Transcription factor prediction analysis of DEPs
To further investigate upstream regulatory mechanisms, transcription factor (
TF
) enrichment analysis was performed using gene sets corresponding to each expression cluster of DEPs. TF prediction was conducted through ChEA3 (
https://maayanlab.cloud/chea3
). For each cluster, the top 10 significantly enriched TFs were selected based on combined ranking scores. TF–target interaction networks were constructed using Cytoscape software (version 3.10.3) to visualize regulatory modules potentially involved in oxidative stress induced proteomic alterations.
Statistical analysis
All experimental data were analyzed using SPSS statistics 26.0 software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Data normality was examined with the Shapiro–Wilk test, and homogeneity of variances was assessed with the Levene test. When assumptions were met, one-way ANOVA was used to compare differences among the four treatment groups, followed by Tukey’s HSD post hoc test to identify pairwise differences. When assumptions were not satisfied, the Kruskal–Wallis test was applied. Statistical significance was defined as
P
< 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Graph generation was performed with GraphPad Prism 9.5.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA).

Discussion
Oxidative stress is a prevalent pathophysiological condition in intensive livestock and poultry production systems, especially under high-density rearing, environmental stressors such as temperature and humidity fluctuations, and ammonia accumulation (
Oke, et al., 2024
;
Surai, et al., 2019
). Among affected organs, the intestinal tract is particularly susceptible because of its high metabolic activity and constant exposure to exogenous stressors. Oxidative damage in the gut compromises nutrient absorption, impairs growth performance, and increases the risk of opportunistic infections and mortality. In vitro, because of its physicochemical attributes, hydrogen peroxide (
H₂O₂
) is widely employed as a model oxidant to induce oxidative stress (
Xu, et al., 2016
). As a small, polar molecule, H₂O₂ readily diffuses across cellular membranes and, upon entry, participates in Fenton chemistry to generate hydroxyl radicals and other reactive oxygen species (
ROS
) (
Wang, et al., 2023b
). These highly reactive molecules trigger lipid peroxidation, protein denaturation, and DNA damage (
Sies and Jones, 2020
). Compared with synthetic agents such as paraquat or tert‑butyl hydroperoxide, H₂O₂ is more physiologically relevant, as it is endogenously produced during aerobic metabolism and inflammatory signaling (
Adler, 2006
). This makes it a more suitable agent for modeling oxidative injury under real-world conditions. In addition to the oxidative inducer, the appropriateness of the epithelial cell model used in this study also warrants consideration. Comparable avian epithelial systems, including primary chicken IECs, two-dimensional enteroids, and intestinal organoids, have been shown to faithfully reproduce principal epithelial lineages such as enterocytes, goblet cells, Paneth-like cells, and enteroendocrine cells (
Ghiselli et al., 2021
;
Orr et al., 2021
). These models also maintain intact epithelial barrier functions, thus supporting the suitability of the present epithelial cell model for mechanistic investigations related to oxidative stress and EV secretion. While our primary culture system is epithelial-enriched and appropriate for investigating IEC-derived EV secretion under oxidative stress, we acknowledge that the exact proportions of epithelial subtypes can vary across preparations (embryonic age and culture conditions), as reported in avian IEC and enteroid studies, therefore, subtype quantification was beyond the scope of the present work. In the present study, H₂O₂ exposure led to a dose-dependent reduction in cell viability, accompanied by a marked downregulation of the mRNA expression of key TJ components, including
ZO-1, claudin-1,
and
occludin
. Cells exposed to 200 μM H₂O₂ showed severe cytotoxicity and transcriptional suppression of the expression of TJ genes. In contrast, 50 and 100 μM H₂O₂ induced only relatively lower reductions in cell viability and moderate changes in gene expression, suggesting a graded cellular response depending on oxidative intensity. This graded response may reflect the dynamic nature of redox adaptation. These results are consistent with previous findings that oxidative stress impairs epithelial barrier integrity by affecting TJ complex regulation via redox-sensitive pathways such as the MAPK, NF-κB, and PI3K/Akt pathways (
Gao, et al., 2023
;
Peng, et al., 2023
). Moreover, in human intestinal epithelial models, mild H₂O₂ exposure caused only reversible damage, whereas higher concentrations led to irreversible cell death and barrier dysfunction (
Watson, et al., 1994
;
Zhao, et al., 2018
). These findings suggest that oxidative stress impairs intestinal epithelial structure by downregulating the expression of TJ-associated genes, ultimately compromising barrier integrity. Moreover, the cellular oxidative stress response appears to be highly dose-dependent, with low-level stress potentially triggering protective mechanisms and high-level stress overwhelming antioxidant capacity, resulting in epithelial damage. At the transcriptional level,
Nrf2
mRNA expression decreased at 50–100 μM relative to that of the control, whereas at 200 μM, it returned to baseline.
HO-1
expression showed a similar nonmonotonic profile. This pattern is consistent with an adaptive response to oxidative stress in which higher ROS burdens can secondarily activate the Nrf2–ARE/HO-1 cytoprotective program (
Huang et al., 2024
). At lower oxidative loads, the antioxidant machinery may initially be suppressed before subsequent compensatory activation, depending on the cellular threshold and exposure duration. Recent work has highlighted the thioredoxin–peroxiredoxin system as an early responder within this adaptive framework (
Oberacker, et al., 2023
). Similarly, the activation of cytoprotective signaling pathways such as the Akt/HO-1 pathway under a low oxidative load has been reported to mitigate apoptosis and maintain epithelial function (
Hu, et al., 2019
). Nonetheless, the initial reduction in Nrf2 expression indicates limited antioxidant defense, which disrupts redox homeostasis and exacerbates the ROS-mediated compromise of the epithelial barrier (
Wang et al., 2023a
;
Wen et al., 2019
). Even with the partial transcriptional rebound at 200 μM, this activation was insufficient to offset injury, as reflected by persistent declines in cell viability and the expression of TJ genes (
ZO-1, claudin-1
, and
occludin
).
EVs act as critical mediators of intercellular communication by transporting a broad spectrum of bioactive cargos, including proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids, that enable the transmission of physiological and pathological signals across tissue microenvironments (
Matsuzaka and Yashiro, 2022
;
Rani, et al., 2023
;
Woith, et al., 2019
). In the intestinal epithelium, EVs have been shown to modulate immune responses, barrier integrity, and epithelial regeneration through their bioactive contents (
Bui, et al., 2018
;
Jiang, et al., 2016
). Increasing amounts of evidence have suggested that the biogenesis and molecular composition of EVs are highly sensitive to external stress cues, particularly oxidative stress, which is a common factor in inflammatory and injury-related conditions (
Chiaradia, et al., 2022
;
Gebremedhn, et al., 2020
;
Rayamajhi, et al., 2023
). Our study provides novel evidence that oxidative stress dynamically reshapes both the secretion kinetics and protein cargo of IEC-derived EVs. We observed a biphasic secretion pattern of EVs upon H₂O₂ stimulation, in which low to moderate oxidative stress (50–100 μM H₂O₂) significantly promoted EV release, whereas a high concentration (200 μM H₂O₂) markedly suppressed it. This biphasic EV secretion pattern is consistent with prior observations suggesting that mild oxidative stress may trigger redox-regulated transcriptional pathways involving HIF-1α, NF-κB, and p53, which have been implicated in regulating the EV biogenesis machinery (
Bhavsar, et al., 2025
;
Sbarigia, et al., 2023
). Previous studies using other cell types have shown that high ROS levels may suppress EV secretion by disrupting Rab-mediated trafficking, partly via PRMT1-dependent pathways (
Chen, et al., 2022
). However, in certain contexts, lysosomal dysfunction may paradoxically increase EV release by blocking degradation (
Gupta, et al., 2024
). These findings support a model in which high ROS levels interfere with vesicle trafficking and docking, thus reducing EV release. These findings suggest a continuum of EV responses related to oxidative intensity: compensatory adaptation at low doses, stress containment at moderate doses, and eventual secretory failure at high oxidative burdens.
GO and KEGG enrichment analyses suggested that low-dose oxidative stress (50 μM H₂O₂) can induce a shift in the functional landscape of EV cargo, reflecting early-stage stress adaptation responses. Consistent with the results of transcriptomic profiling studies, EVs secreted under moderate oxidative conditions accumulate RNA-related molecules, mitochondrial components, and stress-regulated proteins, including small GTPase regulators (
Dellar, et al., 2024
;
Sbarigia, et al., 2023
). These molecular signatures reflect a coordinated cellular response involving RNA metabolism, energy regulation, and membrane trafficking. These vesicles may function as early stress communicators and are capable of priming recipient cells for heightened responsiveness in epithelial or immune contexts (
Chiaradia, et al., 2021
). Under moderate oxidative stress conditions (100 μM H₂O₂), EVs carry proteins enriched in pathways related to protein folding, ER stress, and key signaling cascades such as the MAPK and NOD-like receptor pathways. This pattern suggests that EV cargo packaging is influenced by the activation of the unfolded protein response (
UPR
), which helps cells manage ER overload caused by oxidative imbalance (
Roohi, et al., 2023
;
Simmen, et al., 2010
). Heat shock proteins (
HSPs
), such as Hsp70, are essential mediators of cellular responses to oxidative and ER stress (
Papp, et al., 2003
), but our study revealed no significant changes in Hsp70 expression in EVs under moderate oxidative stress. Instead, we observed a marked downregulation of the expression of other molecular chaperones, including HSP90AB1, HSPD1, and HSP90AB2P. These findings suggest that the composition of EV-associated chaperones may be selectively regulated and does not uniformly reflect all cellular stress-associated HSPs. To further dissect the stress-specific EV response, we performed PPI network analysis across treatment groups. In the EV-L group, central hub proteins such as PDIA3, PGK1, and TRAP1 linked redox homeostasis with energy metabolism and RNA processing-hallmarks of adaptive reprogramming. In contrast, the EV-M network prominently featured HSPA5, CALR, and RPL23A, indicating the activation of ER quality control and translational buffering. These interaction networks reveal a gradual shift in proteome architecture, which is tightly coupled to intracellular stress adaptation or failure mechanisms.
Furthermore, we analyzed 32 differentially expressed EV proteins between the oxidative stress group and the control group. Functional enrichment indicated that these proteins are predominantly involved in protein folding, mRNA splicing, mitochondrial metabolism, and cytoskeletal organization, highlighting that oxidative stress induces functional remodeling of EV cargo. These alterations may compromise the homeostatic and signaling roles of EVs under stress conditions (
Chiaradia, et al., 2021
). PPI network analysis revealed several hub proteins, including HNRNPA3, HSP90AB1, PDIA3, CALR, IQGAP1, ACTN1, and VIM, which exhibited high connectivity and central roles within the network. Many of these proteins, particularly HSP90AB1, HSPD1, and HSPE1, are mitochondrial or ER-associated chaperones involved in proteostasis and stress recovery (
Altieri, 2012
;
Galai, et al., 2020
). The downregulation of the expression of these proteins under oxidative stress may reflect a loss of EV-associated cytoprotective capacity, as chaperones such as HSP70 and HSP90 are key functional components of stress-induced EVs, and their impairment weakens intercellular signaling (
Maio, 2010
;
Niforou, et al., 2014
). Similarly, the expressions of PDIA3 and CALR, two ER-resident proteins involved in calcium buffering and antigen presentation, were also downregulated. These observations align with the literature, indicating that oxidative stress disrupts ER homeostasis, leading to impaired protein folding and a reduced capacity for antigen presentation (
Groenendyk, et al., 2014
). CALR is critical for calcium regulation and acts as a chaperone in the folding of MHC class I-associated peptides, with dysregulation linked to compromised immune signaling under stress conditions (
Bansal, et al., 2023
). In contrast, FABP5 expression was upregulated in EVs derived from stressed cells. As a lipid-binding protein, FABP5 is involved in redox regulation, inflammatory signaling, and membrane homeostasis, and may act as a paracrine signal to modulate recipient cell metabolism under stress conditions (
Gally, et al., 2012
;
Guo, et al., 2021
).
To understand the mechanism underlying EV proteome remodeling under oxidative stress, we focused on upstream transcriptional regulators predicted to modulate key stress-response proteins. One prominent regulatory axis identified through transcription factor enrichment analysis was the XBP1-G6PD/HSP90AB1/ACTG1 axis, which may link UPR signaling to redox control, proteostasis, and cytoskeletal integrity. XBP1, a central component of the UPR, is known to regulate genes involved in ER stress adaptation and oxidative defense (
Shao, et al., 2013
). Our data revealed that all three predicted XBP1s target G6PD, a rate-limiting enzyme associated with the pentose phosphate pathway; HSP90AB1, a molecular chaperone involved in protein folding and stress buffering; and ACTG1, a cytoskeletal protein that is significantly downregulated in EVs from epithelial cells under oxidative stress. These findings suggest that XBP1-driven protective programs are inhibited under sustained stress, limiting the ability of EVs to convey redox-protective or structural support signals to recipient stem/progenitor cells (
Eguchi, et al., 2019
;
Wang, et al., 2014
). Another axis of interest was the predicted transcriptional regulation of FABP5, which was notably upregulated under oxidative stress and is involved in lipid signaling and membrane remodeling. In our analysis, BHLHE40, ZHX1, and NKX1-2 were predicted to be upstream regulators of FABP5. While less studied in EV biology, BHLHE40 has been implicated in circadian and inflammatory regulation under stress conditions (
Zafar, et al., 2021
). The upregulation of FABP5 expression in EVs may reflect a compensatory metabolic response aimed at restoring lipid balance or delivering bioactive lipids to stem cell niches during epithelial injury (
Hotamışlıgil and Bernlohr, 2015
). Finally, we identified SP1 and CENPX as shared regulators of PPIA, a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase with antioxidant and immunomodulatory functions. Decreased PPIA levels in EVs may further compromise stress adaptation in the mucosal microenvironment. SP1 is widely involved in vesicle biogenesis and antioxidant gene regulation, suggesting that it could be a pivotal factor modulating EV composition under stress (
Zelko and Folz, 2004
).
Collectively, these predicted transcriptional axes, particularly those involving XBP1, SP1, and BHLHE40, suggest that EV cargo remodeling under oxidative stress may be partially orchestrated by stress-responsive transcriptional programs. Nevertheless, whether these regulatory pathways represent generalizable mechanisms across epithelial types or oxidative stress models remains to be established. Future studies employing transcription factor perturbation combined with EV proteomics will be crucial to validate the causal role of these regulators and clarify their contribution to epithelial regeneration signaling.
Although our EVs were isolated after 6 h of H₂O₂ exposure, we did not include a specific control to exclude direct oxidant effects on vesicles at the highest dose. Oxidative modifications of membrane lipids and proteins are known to alter bilayer integrity and permeability, which could contribute to EV leakiness or fragmentation under strong oxidant conditions (
Tomita et al., 2019
). We therefore interpret the EV-H findings with caution and list this as a technical limitation. Future work will minimize residual oxidant before EV collection (medium replacement or catalase quenching) and incorporate spike-in and integrity controls to disentangle direct oxidant effects from secretion-driven changes.
Conclusion
Our study demonstrated that oxidative stress altered EV secretion and reshaped EV protein cargo in duck intestinal epithelial cells through transcriptional regulation. Network analysis highlights XBP1–G6PD/HSP90AB1/ACTG1 and SPI1–FABP5 as candidate regulatory routes, consistent with reduced redox buffering and cytoskeletal support and a shift toward lipid-based signaling. These changes may reduce EV-mediated communication with epithelial stem cells under stress. Future studies should validate these nodes and test their functional effects on recipient stem cells to inform nutritional or breeding strategies that support gut health in intensive poultry production.
